summary: DeBar Mountain's lookout began in 1912, got a 35-ft steel Aermotor tower in 1918, closed after 1970 and was removed in 1979.

facts.design: 35-ft steel Aermotor LS40 tower, replacing a 1912 wood tower
facts.status_note: Tower dismantled in 1979; the former tower site is reached by a state-maintained hiking route.

access.note: A hike write-up in the Adirondack Explorer describes a state-maintained route to the former tower site inside the Debar Mountain Wild Forest.

visit.trail_note: Per the Adirondack Explorer hike write-up: 7.4 miles out and back with 1,600 feet of elevation gain, and at least a partial view from the former tower site.

events.note: The Conservation Commission established a lookout at the summit; Wikipedia describes the first structure as a wood fire lookout tower.
A 35-foot steel tower was purchased and erected; Wikipedia identifies it as an Aermotor LS40.
A new observer's cabin was built under the standard 12-by-16-foot plan adopted that year; DeBar was one of five stations to receive one.
State Fire Observer Forest E. Winters is named in a July 1928 item about a snowstorm on the summit.
Lookout operations ended at the close of the 1970 season, per Wikipedia; the Adirondack Explorer says the state closed the tower in 1970.
The tower was dismantled and removed in 1979.

evidence.supports: 1912 lookout established by the Conservation Commission
evidence.quote: 1912: The Conservation Commission established a lookout at this point.
In 1912, the Conservation Department built a wood fire lookout tower on the mountain.
1918: A 35-foot steel tower was purchased and erected.
In 1918, the Conservation Commission replaced it with a 35-foot-tall (11 m) Aermotor LS40 tower.
1922: A new cabin for the observer's living quarters was constructed.

evidence.quote: The other historical and very important occurrence in 1922 was that standard observer's cabin plans were adopted.

evidence.supports: new cabins at DeBar and four other stations
evidence.quote: New cabins were erected at DeBar, Whiteface, Lyon, Poke-Moonshine and Adams.
12’ x 16’ with a roof and siding made of asphalt shingles.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Wikipedia says the Conservation Department built the first wood tower in 1912; the Forest Lookouts page says the Conservation Commission established a lookout that year. Both give 1912; the story says only that a lookout was set up.

sources.title: New York State Chapter newsletter, February 2022

sources.title: Debar Mountain hike cures cabin fever

notes_for_editor: The brief's 1979 removal date is supported by Wikipedia and the Adirondack Explorer. The brief's 'non-conforming structure' reason does not appear in any source read (Forest Lookouts page, 2022 newsletter, Wikipedia, Explorer), so the story omits it; verify or drop it from the record. Staffing evidence is limited to 1928. Sources disagree on Wild Forest size and summit height (Explorer 3,305 ft; Wikipedia 3,317 ft); neither is used. No fire events were found. No source describes what remains of the tower footings or the 1922 cabin on the summit. The Explorer write-up is a hike account, not an agency page; the access level 'public' rests on the state-maintained route and Forest Preserve setting it describes.
